14 	Partial Prerendering (PPR) combines static and dynamic rendering in a single route. At build time, Next.js generates a static HTML shell and a `postponedState` blob for each PPR-enabled route. 15

17 	
18 	## How PPR Works
19 	
20 	### Build time
21 	
22 	For each PPR route, Next.js produces:
23 	
24 	- A **static HTML shell** containing all the content that can be prerendered, with [Suspense](/docs/app/guides/streaming#what-is-streaming) fallbacks where dynamic content will appear.
25 	- A **`postponedState`** value: a serialized string. Treat it as opaque: pass it through without parsing or modifying it. Altering `postponedState` produces incorrect dynamic rendering output.
26 	- An **RSC payload** for the static portions of the page.
27 	
28 	### Request time
29 	
30 	When a request arrives for a PPR route:
31 	
32 	1. The server sends the static HTML shell to the client immediately.
33 	2. The server resumes rendering the dynamic portions using the postponed state.
34 	3. Dynamic content is streamed to the client, allowing React to hydrate the deferred Suspense boundaries.
35 	
36 	The client sees the static shell instantly, then dynamic content appears as it resolves.
37 	
38 	## Storing PPR Artifacts
39 	
40 	Each PPR route requires two artifacts to be stored together:
41 	
42 	1. The static HTML shell.
43 	2. The `postponedState` blob.
44 	
45 	These must be stored and updated atomically. When a PPR route is revalidated (via [time-based](/docs/app/guides/incremental-static-regeneration) or [on-demand revalidation](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/revalidateTag)), Next.js regenerates both the shell and the postponed state together. Serving a new shell with an old postponed state, or vice versa, will produce incorrect dynamic content.
46 	
47 	Use [`requestMeta.onCacheEntryV2`](/docs/app/api-reference/adapters/implementing-ppr-in-an-adapter) in your adapter to observe cache updates and propagate them to your storage backend.
48 	
49 	## Origin-Only Implementation
50 	
51 	**This is the simplest approach and works on every platform that supports streaming HTTP responses.**
52 	
53 	All requests go directly to the Next.js server. The server reads the shell from its local cache, sends it, then renders and streams the dynamic content. This is what `next start` does by default.
54 	
55 	No additional infrastructure is needed. If your platform supports streaming HTTP responses, it supports PPR.
56 	
57 	## CDN Shell + Origin Compute
58 	
59 	For better TTFB, the static HTML shell can be cached at the CDN edge. When a request arrives:

18:Next.js takes a different approach: **the boundary between static and dynamic is at the component level, not the route level.** A single page can have a static shell that loads instantly and dynamic sections that stream in as they resolve. A cached function can live inside a dynamic route. A static page can be updated without a redeploy.
20:This is what Partial Prerendering, [Cache Components](/docs/app/getting-started/caching) (`use cache`), and [on-demand revalidation](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/revalidateTag) enable. They are not incremental features: they represent a rendering model that treats static and dynamic as a spectrum rather than a binary choice.
26:- **Faster perceived load times.** The static shell renders immediately while dynamic content streams in. Users see useful content right away instead of waiting for the entire page to render.
44:This is the approach Next.js takes. Static and dynamic content coexist within a single streaming response. A page can have a static shell that loads instantly, a cached function that revalidates independently, and a dynamic section that streams in as it resolves, all without the developer splitting anything into separate routes or client-side fetches.
55:- **PPR shell delivery at CDN latency** can require additional platform integration to store the static shell separately and resume dynamic rendering correctly. See [PPR Platform Guide](/docs/app/guides/ppr-platform-guide) for implementation details.

516	
517	{/* TODO: diagram — before/after illustration showing a single high-up Suspense boundary being refined down to smaller boundaries closer to the data */}
518	
519	Validation passing means the navigation is instant. It does not mean the loading states are good. A `<Suspense>` boundary placed high in the tree (say, wrapping the whole page) might satisfy validation, but it replaces most of the page with a single fallback on every navigation.
520	
521	The best loading states keep as much real, cached content visible as possible and only show fallbacks where data is actually in flight. 526	
527	At a high level, an agent optimizes a single navigation like this:
528	
529	- **Observe**: read validation insights and choose the exact navigation and UI that should appear immediately.
530	- **Test**: confirm the target UI renders normally, then write an `instant()` test and verify that it fails before changing the route.

310	## Prevent regressions with e2e tests
311	
312	Validation catches structural problems during development, but as the codebase grows, the structural checks can only tell you that a shell exists. They can't tell you whether the right content is in it. E2E tests close that gap: they assert on what the user actually sees when the navigation completes, catching regressions before they ship.
313	
314	The [`@next/playwright`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@next/playwright) package includes an `instant()` helper for this. Install it alongside `@playwright/test`:
315	
316	```bash package="pnpm"
317	pnpm add -D @next/playwright @playwright/test
318	```
319	
320	```bash package="npm"
321	npm install -D @next/playwright @playwright/test
322	```
323	
324	```bash package="yarn"
325	yarn add -D @next/playwright @playwright/test
326	```
327	
328	```bash package="bun"
329	bun add -D @next/playwright @playwright/test
330	```
331	
332	A route can be reached two ways, and a `<Suspense>` boundary can cover one without covering the other:
333	
334	- **Initial page load**: Use `page.goto()` to test the static UI from the document response.
335	- **Client navigation**: Click a `<Link>` to test the destination's prefetched UI. [Per-link prefetching](/docs/app/guides/optimizing-prefetching) can add request-specific content to this UI.
336	
337	```typescript filename="e2e/navigation.test.ts" highlight={6-14,20-25}
338	import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test'
339	import { instant } from '@next/playwright'
340	
341	test.describe('Product page (/store/[slug])', () => {
342	  test('is instant on an initial page load', async ({ page, baseURL }) => {
343	    await instant(
344	      page,
345	      async () => {
346	        await page.goto('/store/hats')
347	        await expect(page.locator('h1')).toContainText('Baseball Cap')
348	        await expect(page.getByText('In stock')).toHaveCount(0)
349	      },

Those sections still share one request-memoized fetch, so they do not fan out into extra calls.

`npx tsc --noEmit && npx next build` finished with exit code 0. `/` is a partial prerender: the static HTML includes `Dashboard`, the card and chart headings, and the section fallbacks, while the API data stays out of the shell.
